scenes.title: Which High School
scenes.text:
Eighth grade ends with a decision that feels bigger than it should. Most of {name}'s classmates will go to the high school the district assigns: the big one by the highway, with a marching band and a parking lot that floods every April.

There are other doors, if {name} can get through them. The region's selective public high school admits students by entrance exam, and some families have paid for test prep since sixth grade. A private school across town has small classes, a college counselor for every grade, and tuition that some families pay without blinking and others can't pay at all.

{name} has a practice booklet from the library and a lot of opinions.

textVariants.append: The selective school and the private school are both a long drive away.

choices.label: {Subj} goes to the assigned public high school
choices.description: Close to home, with most of {poss} middle school friends.
choices.outcome: Ninth grade at the big school is loud, crowded, and familiar. {name} knows half the faces in the hallway by October.

choices.label: {Subj} takes the entrance exam for the selective public school
choices.description: Admission by test score. Some applicants have had years of paid test prep.

terms.label: tutoring and test prep
terms.missingLabel: paid test prep or a tutor

choices.authorFlag: Selective high school odds are placeholders; no source yet.

choices.label: The family applies to a private high school
choices.description: Average private high school tuition: about {usd:private-school:averageTuition.values.secondary.value} a year.

terms.label: tuition of more than a fifth of the family's income, so it depends on a scarce scholarship

choices.authorFlag: Admission (0.8) and scholarship odds are placeholders. The 20%-of-income cutoff reuses the affordability rule in state-model.md.

scenes.title: The Letter
scenes.textIfSuccess: The letter from {college} comes in March, and it's a yes. {name} reads the list of first-week events twice, then texts everyone {subj} knows.
scenes.textIfFailure: The letter from {college} comes in March. It's a no, politely worded. Most of {name}'s friends are going to the assigned school anyway, and by summer it stops stinging.

scenes.title: Other Doors
scenes.text: One door closed. {name} and {poss} family look at the ones still open.

scenes.title: The Schedule
scenes.text:
The ninth-grade course catalog is forty pages long, and {name} reads more of it than anyone expected. Some classes are labeled honors or AP and count for more in a GPA. Some lead to certifications in welding, nursing assistance, or coding. A few let students take classes at the community college for free and leave high school with college credits.

The counselor has fifteen minutes for each student. {name}'s friends are comparing schedules in the group chat, and everyone has a different theory about what colleges want.

textVariants.append: {Poss} school offers only a handful of AP classes, and some of them meet before first period.

choices.label: {Subj} loads up on AP and honors classes
choices.outcome: {name}'s backpack weighs a ton, and {subj} learns what three hours of homework feels like. The transcript looks strong.

choices.label: {Subj} takes every AP class {poss} school offers
choices.authorFlag: Which schools offer few AP classes is modeled from place flags; needs a statistic on AP access by school poverty or rurality (college_board_ap or nces_coe).
choices.outcome: {name} takes all of them. It's a strong transcript for {poss} school, and a shorter one than students at schools with long AP lists.

choices.label: {Subj} takes a balanced schedule with some honors classes
choices.outcome: {name} gets enough sleep most nights and still has a few classes that push {obj}.

choices.label: {Subj} joins the career and technical track
choices.description: Hands-on classes that can end in a certification.
choices.outcome: {name} spends afternoons in a shop or a lab with real equipment, and finds a knack for something {subj} never had the chance to try.

choices.label: {Subj} takes free classes at the community college
choices.description: College credits before graduation, and a long bus ride twice a week.
choices.outcome: {name} sits in a lecture hall with adults twice {poss} age, takes better notes than most of them, and banks a semester of credits.

choices.label: {Subj} does what it takes to graduate, and no more
choices.outcome: {name} passes everything and keeps {poss} afternoons. A few options quietly narrow, and {subj} won't notice which ones until later.

scenes.title: Tryouts
scenes.text:
The sign-up sheet for fall tryouts goes up outside the gym in the second week of ninth grade. A lot of the names on it belong to kids who have played on club teams since elementary school, with private coaches, summer camps, and parents who drive them to tournaments three states away.

There are other ways to play. A club team in the next town holds showcases where college coaches sit in the bleachers with clipboards, if a family can cover the fees, the hotel nights, and the gas. The intramural league at school costs nothing and meets twice a week.

{name} looks at the sheet for a long time.

textVariants.append: {Subj}’s been playing since middle school, and {poss} old teammates are already on the list.
Practice would run until six, and someone would have to pick up the younger kids.

choices.label: {Subj} tries out for the school team
choices.description: No club fees, practice every day after school.

terms.label: years of playing on a team
sticking with one thing for years

choices.authorFlag: Tryout odds are placeholders; no source yet.

choices.label: {Subj} plays for a club team with college showcases
choices.description: Families earning $100,000 or more spend about {stat:youth_sports_spending_high_income} a year on a child’s main sport.

availability.stretchNote: Young athletes from families earning $100,000 or more are about twice as likely to play club or travel ({stat:travel_club_share_high_income}) as those from families earning under $50,000 ({stat:travel_club_share_low_income}).

choices.authorFlag: Stretch for the two lowest brackets, as at D7. No club price is in the data.
choices.outcome: The schedule is brutal and the team is good. Some weekends there are more college coaches in the stands than parents.

choices.label: {Subj} plays intramural and pickup games
choices.description: Free, twice a week, and nobody keeps stats.
choices.outcome: Tuesday and Thursday nights in the gym, mixed teams, loud and a little chaotic. It’s the best part of {name}’s week.

choices.label: {Subj} skips sports this year
choices.description: More time for school, work, or family.
choices.outcome: {name} gets {poss} afternoons back. Some of them go to homework. Some go to nothing in particular, which also has its uses.

scenes.title: The Roster
scenes.textIfSuccess: The roster goes up on the gym door on Friday afternoon, and {name}’s name is on it, third from the bottom. Practice starts Monday at 3:15. {Subj} wears {poss} new practice jersey around the house all weekend.
scenes.textIfFailure:
The roster goes up on the gym door on Friday afternoon. {name} reads it twice. {Poss} name isn’t there.

A few friends made it. The coach says to come back next year and work on the basics.

scenes.title: Other Ways to Play
scenes.text: Getting cut stings for about a week. Then the question comes back: there are still other ways to play, or {name} can let sports go and use the time for something else.

scenes.title: Everything Else
scenes.text:
Between classes and sleep, there are a few hours left in the week, and everyone has a claim on them. Student government needs a treasurer. The theater is casting the spring musical. The robotics team is short a programmer. The grocery store on the corner is hiring, and it pays every two weeks.

At home, someone has to get the younger kids to bed when the grown-ups work late. And {name}'s friends would like to see {obj} sometime, with no schedule at all.

College applications will ask about all of it, though they won't weigh it all the same.

textVariants.append: Practice already takes every afternoon until six.
{Subj}'s been the one at home after school for years.

choices.label: {Subj} runs for student government and joins debate
choices.outcome: {name} learns to give a speech without {poss} hands shaking and to run a meeting that ends on time. Teachers start learning {poss} name.

choices.label: {Subj} joins the theater crew and the choir
choices.outcome: {name} spends spring evenings in a dark auditorium, painting sets and learning harmonies. The cast party is the best night of the year.

choices.label: {Subj} joins the robotics team or an academic competition
choices.outcome: Weekends become regionals, in gyms full of robots or buzzers. {name}'s team places third and celebrates like it won.

choices.label: {Subj} gets a part-time job
choices.description: A paycheck every two weeks, and less time for homework.
choices.outcome: {name} learns the register, the regulars, and how to smile through a double shift. {Subj} saves most of every paycheck.

choices.label: {Subj} takes care of things at home
choices.description: Dinner, homework help, and bedtime for the younger kids.
choices.outcome: {name} gets the younger kids fed, bathed, and to bed most nights. It's real work, and there's no line for it on a college application.

choices.label: {Subj} keeps {poss} afternoons free for friends
choices.outcome: Long afternoons at someone's house, drives to nowhere, a group chat that never sleeps. {name} will remember these people for a long time.

scenes.title: Friday Night
scenes.text:
Jordan's parents are out of town, and by third period everyone knows it. By lunch the group chat has a playlist. By the last bell somebody's older brother has agreed to "help with supplies," which everyone understands to mean exactly what it sounds like.

{name} has a chemistry test Monday. {Subj} also has a feeling, the kind that only comes at sixteen, that this is one of those nights people will talk about for years, and that {subj}'ll either be in the stories or hear them secondhand.

textVariants.append: Coach has a 7 a.m. practice tomorrow, and he notices who's tired.
{Subj} is on the schedule at the grocery store at 9.

choices.label: {Subj} goes and stays until the end
choices.outcome: {name} gets home at 2:40. It's the best night of the year, and the chemistry test goes about as well as anyone would expect.

choices.label: {Subj} shows up for an hour, then heads home
choices.outcome: {Subj}'s there long enough to be in the photos and home in time to sleep. Nobody remembers that {subj} left.

choices.label: {Subj} stays home tonight
choices.outcome: {Subj} aces the test. On Monday, everyone has an inside joke {subj} doesn't get.

choices.label: {Subj} invites a few friends over instead
choices.outcome: Five friends, two pizzas, a movie nobody watches. It's quieter, and {subj}'ll remember it longer than {subj} expects.

researchNote.title: Who Gets Help Applying
researchNote.text: School counselors help students choose classes, find scholarships, and apply to college. The national average is {stat:counselor_ratio} students per counselor, compared with the {stat:counselor_ratio_recommended} the American School Counselor Association recommends. Families who can pay for private admissions help can make up the difference. Many can't.
